title: Judas and Pilate's wife (Matthew 27:1–26)
hook: silver handed back, a warning from a dream, and a bowl of water before the crowd
carry: have nothing to do with him
tomorrow: darkness over the land, a torn curtain, and a soldier says what?

segments.voice: A rooster, a remembered word, and a man who went out: he wept bitterly. Now morning comes, and two more people face what they've done.

Cool water running over your hands at a sink: an ordinary feeling from any day. This chapter has a washing that isn't ordinary. But first, morning. Judas sees that Jesus is condemned and brings the thirty pieces of silver back to the chief priests and elders: "I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood." The answer is short and cold: "What is that to us? see thou to that." Hold onto that phrase. It comes back, with water.
screen: `WATER OVER YOUR HANDS.` → `I HAVE BETRAYED THE INNOCENT BLOOD.` → `SEE THOU TO THAT.`

segments.voice: Judas throws the silver down in the Temple and goes and hangs himself. Matthew tells it in one sentence, and this lesson will too. If that lands heavy today, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help wherever you are. Now Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor. He asks Jesus, "Art thou the King of the Jews?" Jesus says, "Thou sayest," and then nothing more, "insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly." Pilate offers the crowd a choice, Barabbas or Jesus. And while he sits on the judgment seat, a message comes from his wife: "Have thou nothing to do with that just man: for I have suffered many things this day in a dream because of him." Matthew never names her, and she never appears again. The crowd calls for crucifixion. Then the water. Pilate takes it and washes his hands before the multitude: "I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it." Hear the echo. The priests to Judas: see thou to that. Pilate to the crowd: see ye to it. Each hands the weight to someone else. Washing hands to declare innocence was an old sign; Israel's law has elders do it. But Pilate still releases Barabbas and delivers Jesus to be crucified. The water is cool, and his hands are not clean of it.
screen: `JUDAS: THE SILVER THROWN DOWN.` · `HE ANSWERED NEVER A WORD.` · `A WARNING FROM A DREAM.` · `SEE YE TO IT.` · then, large: `HAVE NOTHING TO DO WITH HIM.`

segments.voice: If there's a sink nearby, run cool water over your hands and feel it; if not, press your palms together. Name one person you're tempted to call not my problem. Then, instead of washing them off, hold your hands cupped and open, as if they were still in them. Breathe there for a while, hands open, keeping them.
Judas and Pilate's wife. A man who tried to give the silver back, and a woman who sent a warning her husband washed away.
Your line: have nothing to do with him, her warning, and the water couldn't wash it out. Go gently.

what a scholar hears: the echo 'see thou to that' (27:4) and 'see ye to it' (27:24); a handwashing that recalls the elders' rite in Deuteronomy 21:6–7; and the wife's ὄναρ, a dream, as in Joseph's dreams in chapters 1 and 2.

notes: Hard scene, gentle handling: Judas' death (27:5) is told in one sentence, with the 988 / local emergency line right after it. Parents listening with children may want to be close for this day. A Keeper should confirm the tone.

Matthew 27:25 is left out on purpose: it has a long history of being misused against Jewish people. The lesson says only 'the crowd' and 'the multitude', and Pilate delivers Jesus to be crucified (27:26).
'Washing hands to declare innocence was an old sign; Israel's law has elders do it' rests on Deuteronomy 21:6–7 (paraphrased); confirm the link is fair.
The 'see thou to that' / 'see ye to it' echo (27:4, 27:24) is the lesson's observation from the KJV wording; a scholar may confirm the Greek echoes too.
Pilate's wife is unnamed in Matthew; later tradition gives her a name, which the lesson leaves out.
Senses shape: water over the hands carries the idea; the practice is physical (water, or palms pressed, then hands cupped open).
